5. A first recipe

David Sarrat González

Source: vignettes/book-05-recipe.Rmd
book-05-recipe.Rmd

What you will learn

Build education and cause-of-death columns, predict their output, and request category counts.

You need: the client packages and the Opal login from Getting started. This chapter uses omop.questionnaire, the synthetic questionnaire study described there.

Start this chapter

Log in first:

library(dsOMOPClient)
conns <- ds.omop.login("https://localhost:8443", user = "administrator",
  password = "password", resource = "omop.questionnaire", server = "site")$conns

The connection is ready; conns identifies the server used by the analysis calls.

The questionnaire has 48 people. Of these, 24 answered the education question (twice each), 36 have a recorded death, and 12 have neither education nor death. These are the teaching data described in Getting started.

Select the education question

An event describes records of interest. It is a definition on your computer, not a downloaded table. We have switched from chapter 4’s GiBleed asthma search to the questionnaire dataset. First look up its education question by concept:

question <- ds.omop.concept.lookup(900001L, conns = conns)
question$pooled[c("concept_id", "concept_name")]
concept_id concept_name
900001 Education question

Education question is concept 900001, found in chapter 4. Use that ID to select observations:

education_event <- omop_event("observation", concepts = 900001L)

The server will select observations whose question is Education question.

Choose one answer per person

A reducer turns possibly many records into one value. Use the latest nonmissing coded answer, ordered by the observation date:

education <- omop_variable(
  event = education_event,
  reducer = omop_reduce("last_value", value = "value_as_concept_id"))
education
#> omop_variable: <unnamed>
#>    last_value of observation

This makes one categorical column. It does not create a separate binary column for every education level. A same-date tie uses the documented deterministic record ordering; it does not mean “largest answer ID”.

Add cause of death 

cause <- omop_variable(
  event = omop_event("death"),
  reducer = omop_reduce("first_value", value = "cause_concept_id"))

Here the value comes from cause_concept_id. Do not substitute cause_source_value: that is the verbatim source code, such as an ICD-10 code, rather than the standard concept used for translated categories. Source-value fields are blocked on this route.

Describe a wide table

Wide means one column per variable. Person grain means one row per person. The native all-person population retains people who have neither answer nor death.

people <- omop_recipe(
  variables = list(education = education, cause_of_death = cause),
  outputs = omop_output("people", format = "wide", grain = "person"))

person_id is included automatically as a pseudonym. Missing records produce missing values. The roster does not require an extra identifier variable.

Predict: read the recipe explanation

Before running, predict 48 rows and three columns: the automatic person key, education and cause of death. Education should have 24 missing values. Both variables read all recorded history because no time window restricts them.

explained <- recipe_explain(people, conns = conns)
writeLines(head(explained$text, 9))
#> Recipe plan
#> Population 'base' (criteria): none
#> Variables:
#>   education: last_value of event 'obs_900001' (value 'value_as_concept_id') over any time; missing = "skip"
#>   cause_of_death: first_value of event 'death' (value 'cause_concept_id') over any time; missing = "skip"
#> Output 'people' [wide] rows 'base', grain person
#> Published: people
#> Defaults relied on:
#>   - variable 'education': rows with a NULL value are skipped before the row is selected (missing = "skip")

Read this short opening in order: the population sets one row per person; education takes the last coded observation answer; cause_of_death takes the first coded death cause; the output arranges them as columns. The remaining explanation describes technical defaults; these are not observed patient counts.

Run: assign the result 

recipe_execute(people, out = c(people = "D_people"), conns = conns)

Nothing comes back to you: the output named people is now D_people, a table kept on the server. Concept-valued columns are labelled factors because of their declared type. The names education and cause_of_death need no _concept_id suffix.

Verify: check what you got

Use DSI::datashield.symbols() to list assigned server objects. Then check the size, column names, type and missingness. These calls return metadata or checked aggregates; they never retrieve patient rows.

DSI::datashield.symbols(conns)
#> $site
#> [1] "D_people" "omop"

D_people is present alongside the omop resource handle: the extraction has created a private analysis table.

dsBaseClient::ds.dim("D_people", datasources = conns)
#> $`dimensions of D_people in site`
#> [1] 48  3
#>
#> $`dimensions of D_people in combined studies`
#> [1] 48  3

The 48 rows correspond to all 48 people, including people with missing answers. The three columns match the prediction.

dsBaseClient::ds.colnames("D_people", datasources = conns)
#> $site
#> [1] "person_id"      "education"      "cause_of_death"

person_id is the automatic protected key; the other two columns are the variables we requested.

dsBaseClient::ds.class("D_people$education", datasources = conns)
#> $site
#> [1] "dsomop_concept_factor" "factor"

Education is a factor, which stores categories. dsomop_concept_factor records that these categories come from OMOP concepts.

dsBaseClient::ds.numNA("D_people$education", datasources = conns)
#> $site
#> [1] 24

The 24 missing values are people with no education answer. The next category table completes the predict, run, verify loop. In later lessons, choose the one check that helps answer the current question.

Count the education categories 

education_table_result <- dsBaseClient::ds.table("D_people$education", useNA = "no", datasources = conns)
education_table_result$output.list$TABLES.COMBINED_all.sources_counts
#> D_people$education
#>  Secondary education University education
#>                   12                   12

There are 12 people whose latest answer is Secondary education and 12 whose latest answer is University education. Every respondent gave both answers at different times; these are counts of the selected latest answer, not everyone who ever gave each answer. useNA = "no" leaves out the 24 missing values.

Count causes 

ds.omop.table("D_people", "cause_of_death", conns = conns)
#> D_people$cause_of_death
#> Myocardial infarction             Pneumonia
#>                    24                    12

The table shows 24 myocardial infarctions and 12 pneumonias. ds.omop.table() is a shortcut that also retains categories with zero people. Missing causes are excluded here; the exercise below will include them. Absence of a death record is not proof of survival.

Give a question your own yes/no labels

Chapter 4 identifies Fever question as 900002, Yes as 900301, and No as 900302. Here is a label map keyed by those answer IDs:

fever <- omop_variable(
  event = omop_event("observation", concepts = 900002L),
  reducer = omop_reduce("last_value", value = "value_as_concept_id"),
  labels = c("900301" = "yes", "900302" = "no"))

The map is keyed by answer concepts. It changes presentation, not which question is selected. Missing fever answers remain missing; they do not become “no”.

answers <- omop_recipe(
  variables = list(education = education, fever = fever, cause_of_death = cause),
  outputs = omop_output("people", format = "wide", grain = "person"))
recipe_execute(answers, out = c(people = "D_answers"), conns = conns)
yes_no_result <- dsBaseClient::ds.table("D_answers$fever", useNA = "no", datasources = conns)
yes_no_result$output.list$TABLES.COMBINED_all.sources_counts
#> D_answers$fever
#> yes  no
#>  12  12

The table contains 12 “yes” and 12 “no” answers, using your lower-case labels. The other 24 people did not answer; they are excluded by useNA = "no". See chapter 10 for the same operation across two different vocabularies.

Exercise 1: first answer instead of last

Take each person’s first education answer. Do the totals for each category reveal that people changed answers?

Solution

first_education <- omop_variable(event = education_event,
  reducer = omop_reduce("first_value", value = "value_as_concept_id"))
comparison <- omop_recipe(variables = list(first = first_education, last = education),
  outputs = omop_output("people", format = "wide", grain = "person"))
recipe_execute(comparison, out = c(people = "D_education_change"), conns = conns)
dsBaseClient::ds.table(
  "D_education_change$first", "D_education_change$last", useNA = "no",
  datasources = conns)$output.list$TABLES.COMBINED_all.sources_counts
Secondary education University education
Secondary education 0 12
University education 12 0

Rows show first answers and columns show last answers. The off-diagonal cells show 12 people changing from Secondary to University and 12 changing in the opposite direction. The first and last category totals are both 12/12, so those totals alone hide every respondent’s change.

Exercise 2: include missing causes

Count causes with dsBase and include people without a coded cause.

Solution

dsBaseClient::ds.table("D_people$cause_of_death",
  useNA = "always", datasources = conns)$output.list$TABLES.COMBINED_all.sources_counts
#> D_people$cause_of_death
#> Myocardial infarction             Pneumonia                    NA
#>                    24                    12                    12

The 24 myocardial infarctions, 12 pneumonias and 12 missing causes account for all 48 people. Missing is not another coded cause and does not establish survival.

Exercise 3: why not use the source code?

Try compiling a cause variable based on cause_source_value. Does renaming it make that source field available?

Solution

source_cause <- omop_recipe(variables = list(cause = omop_variable(
  event = omop_event("death"),
  reducer = omop_reduce("first_value", value = "cause_source_value"))))
recipe_to_plan(source_cause)
#> Error:
#> ! Disclosive: the plan requests blocked (class-1) column(s) that the server can never release or filter on: cause_source_value (variable 'cause' reducer value).

The source-value field is blocked before execution. A new variable name does not change its protection; use cause_concept_id for the coded cause.

Recap

An event selects records, a reducer selects a value, and a wide output arranges private rows. Only the aggregate returns to you.
